title: Choosing the Right Carrier Size for Your Dog
excerpt: How to measure your dog properly, read a carrier's size listing correctly, and match the right size category so it's neither too snug nor too loose.
content:
Choosing a pet carrier is not simply about finding one that fits your dog today. The right carrier needs to give them enough room to sit, stand and turn round, hold up to their actual weight, and still feel secure rather than cavernous. Getting the size wrong in either direction, too snug or too loose, tends to show up the first time your dog actually has to spend more than a few minutes inside.

This guide walks through how to measure your dog properly, what a carrier's size listing actually tells you, and how to match that against the right category, whether your dog is a small breed, a growing puppy, or already at the larger end of the scale.

## How to Measure Your Dog Properly

Three measurements matter here, and none of them is your dog's breed.

### Length, Height and Width

Measure your dog from the tip of their nose to the base of their tail for length, from the floor to the top of their head or ears (whichever is taller) for height, and across their shoulders for width. Add a few centimetres to each figure for comfortable movement, but resist the urge to add a lot more "just in case", since a carrier with too much spare space can leave a dog feeling less secure once it's actually moving.

If your dog naturally sits between two sizes, it's generally worth sizing up slightly for longer journeys and keeping it snugger for short trips, since a closer fit tends to help dogs feel calmer when the carrier itself is in motion.

### Why Weight Alone Isn't Enough

A carrier's maximum weight capacity tells you what the base, handles and stitching can safely support, not whether your dog will actually fit comfortably inside. A carrier can look roomy enough in photos while still being under-built for a heavier dog's real weight, and equally, a dog can be well under the weight limit while still being too long or too tall for the internal space. Check both figures independently rather than assuming one implies the other.

## Matching Size to the Right Category

Once you have your dog's measurements and weight, shopping within the right size band is usually quicker than browsing everything at once. Our [small dog carriers](/carriers/dog-carriers/small-dog-carriers) range covers dogs up to around 10kg, [medium dog carriers](/carriers/dog-carriers/medium-dog-carriers) covers roughly 10kg to 25kg, and [large dog carriers](/carriers/dog-carriers/large-dog-carriers) is built with a sturdier frame for anything heavier. If your dog is right on a boundary, checking a specific product's stated capacity matters more than the category label itself.

## If Your Dog Is Still a Puppy

A young puppy who hasn't reached their adult size yet is usually better served by a carrier sized to where they are right now rather than where they'll eventually end up. Our [puppy carriers](/carriers/dog-carriers/puppy-carriers) range is built specifically around that smaller, still-growing stage, with a snugger, more reassuring shape than an adult-sized carrier with a lot of unused space. Plan to move up once they're closer to their full adult weight rather than buying ahead.

## Final Thoughts

Getting the size right comes down to your dog's actual measurements and weight, checked properly against a carrier's stated dimensions and capacity, rather than a guess based on breed or age. Take the time to measure your dog rather than estimating, and treat a slightly snugger fit as reassuring rather than restrictive. It's a five-minute job that makes every carrier journey afterwards noticeably easier for both of you.

faqs.answer: Only once they're fully grown. For a puppy, plan to move up in size as they approach their adult weight rather than buying one carrier meant to last indefinitely.

title: Helping a Nervous Cat Get Used to a Carrier
excerpt: Why cats associate the carrier with stress, and the practical groundwork that helps them feel calmer about it, from choosing the right carrier to preparing for travel day.
content:
Most cats only encounter their carrier a handful of times a year, almost always right before something unfamiliar and slightly stressful happens. Without more regular, low-stakes exposure, the carrier itself becomes a signal that something unsettling is about to happen, rather than just another object in the house. A little groundwork between trips can genuinely change how your cat feels about it.

## Why Cats React This Way

Cats build associations quickly, and a carrier that only appears before a vet visit or a journey gets linked to that experience rather than to anything neutral. This is a learned response, not a fixed personality trait, which is exactly why it can be gradually unlearned with the right approach.

## Getting the Carrier Ready Before Travel Day

### Leave It Out, Not Just Before a Trip

Leave the carrier out in a quiet corner of the house for a week or two before you actually need it, ideally with a soft blanket inside and a few treats scattered near the entrance. Let your cat investigate in their own time rather than pushing them towards it. Repeating this every so often, not only right before a trip, is what actually breaks the specific association with stress.

### Choose a Carrier That Helps Rather Than Hinders

A carrier with a top-loading opening tends to cause far less stress than one with only a front door, since you can lower your cat in gently rather than having to push them through a narrow gap. Our [cat carriers](/carriers/cat-carriers) range is built with this kind of calmer handling in mind, and our [soft-sided cat carriers](/carriers/cat-carriers/soft-sided-cat-carriers) range is a reasonable starting point if your cat hasn't had a carrier before, since the give in the fabric tends to feel less clinical than a hard shell.

## Building Positive Associations Gradually

Rather than only using the carrier right before you need it, try feeding your cat a meal near it, or placing treats and toys just inside the doorway over several days. Some owners find it helps to get their cat used to being closed inside for a few seconds at a time in short, calm sessions well before travel day, rather than the first time the door shuts being on the way to the vet.

## Signs Your Cat Is Getting More Comfortable

Watch for your cat choosing to sleep in or near the carrier, walking past it without reacting, or investigating it on their own rather than needing to be coaxed. These are good signs the groundwork is working, even if actual travel is still likely to feel different to a cat who generally prefers familiar surroundings.

## On the Day of Travel

Covering part of the carrier with a light cloth during the journey can help too, since it reduces visual stimulation and gives your cat a smaller, calmer space to settle into. Keep handling brief and matter-of-fact rather than making a fuss over them, since cats often pick up on an owner's own tension around the carrier more than the carrier itself.

## If a Vet Visit Is the Reason You're Here

If it's specifically an upcoming vet appointment prompting this, our [pet carriers for vet visits](/carriers/pet-carriers-for-vet-visits) range picks out designs suited to that shorter, more clinical kind of trip across every pet we carry, not just cats.

## Final Thoughts

A carrier doesn't have to mean stress for your cat, but that usually takes a bit of groundwork done well before travel day, not just a calmer approach on the day itself. Regular, low-pressure exposure at home, paired with a design that makes handling easier for both of you, tends to make the biggest difference over time.

faqs.answer: This varies a lot between cats. Some settle within a week or two of regular, low-pressure exposure, while others take longer. Consistency matters more than speed here.

faqs.question: Should I feed my cat near the carrier?
faqs.answer: Yes, many owners find that feeding meals or treats near or inside the carrier helps build a positive association over time, rather than the carrier only appearing before something stressful.

faqs.answer: For most cats, yes. It lets you lower them in gently rather than pushing them through a narrow front door, which tends to cause far less resistance and stress.

faqs.answer: Go back a step and spend longer on low-pressure exposure at home before your next attempt. If a vet visit can't wait, gently guiding rather than forcing your cat in, and keeping the experience as calm as possible, is the practical option on the day.

faqs.question: Should I cover the carrier during travel?
faqs.answer: Many cats find a light cover over part of the carrier reassuring, since it reduces visual stimulation. Make sure it doesn't block ventilation panels.

title: Flying with Your Pet: What UK Airlines Expect
excerpt: What most UK airlines look for in an in-cabin pet carrier, why requirements vary between operators, and how to prepare properly before you fly.
content:
If you're planning to fly with a small pet, the carrier you choose matters just as much as the ticket you book. Most UK airlines that allow pets in the cabin set their own maximum carrier dimensions and combined pet-and-carrier weight limits, and these can differ quite a bit between operators, sometimes even between two airlines that otherwise seem similar.

This guide covers what most airlines generally look for, how to prepare properly, and why checking directly with your specific airline before booking matters more than relying on a carrier labelled "airline approved" alone.

## What Most Airlines Look For

### Carrier Dimensions and Weight

As a general rule, airlines that allow pets in the cabin expect a carrier low and flat enough to fit fully under the seat in front of you, often with a strict height limit. Combined pet-and-carrier weight limits are also common, meaning the carrier's own weight can count towards the total, not just your pet's.

### Ventilation and Construction

A soft-sided carrier that can compress slightly tends to fare better than a rigid one for cabin travel, since rigid carriers are rarely accepted in the cabin, though they may suit hold travel with the right preparation. Mesh panelling for airflow matters too, particularly since your pet may be inside for the full duration of the flight.

### Secure Closures

A secure, lockable zip is worth checking specifically. Airport handling is busy, and a closure that can't be fixed properly shut is a genuine risk during boarding, not just an inconvenience.

## Confirming Rules With Your Airline

Always confirm pet travel rules directly with your airline before booking, ideally at the time of booking rather than afterwards, since space for pets in the cabin is usually limited and allocated on a first-come basis. Airline and transport-provider requirements can change, so treat any general guidance, including this article, as a starting point rather than a guarantee. We're not able to confirm that any specific carrier meets a particular airline's requirements, so always check the current published guidelines for your airline before you travel.

## Choosing the Right Carrier for Cabin Travel

Our [airline approved pet carriers](/carriers/pet-airline-approved-carriers) range covers cabin-friendly designs across every pet type, built around the kind of low, flat profile most airlines expect. For dogs and cats specifically, our [airline approved dog carriers](/carriers/dog-carriers/airline-approved-dog-carriers) and [airline approved cat carriers](/carriers/cat-carriers/airline-approved-cat-carriers) ranges are sized around each animal's typical proportions rather than being a single one-size-fits-all design.

## Preparing Before You Travel

Get your pet used to the specific carrier well before the flight, not for the first time at the airport. A pet who already associates the carrier with calm, familiar time at home tends to cope with the noise and unfamiliar environment of an airport considerably better than one encountering it all for the first time on travel day.

## If You're Travelling Internationally

Pet travel across borders often involves additional requirements beyond the airline's own carrier rules, such as microchipping, vaccination records or specific paperwork depending on the destination. These requirements vary by country and can change, so check the current guidance for your specific destination well ahead of your trip, in addition to your airline's cabin carrier rules.

## Beyond the Flight Itself

Don't forget the journey to and from the airport too. If you're driving, our [pet carriers for car travel](/carriers/pet-car-travel-carriers) range covers carriers built to stay stable and properly secured on the back seat or in the boot, which matters just as much as the cabin-approved carrier once you're actually on the road.

## Final Thoughts

Flying with a pet comes down to matching your carrier to your specific airline's published requirements, not a general sense of what counts as cabin-friendly, and confirming those requirements directly before you book rather than after. A well-prepared, properly sized carrier and a pet who's already comfortable inside it will make the day considerably less stressful for you both.

faqs.answer: This depends on your airline's own pet policy, your pet's weight, and the destination's import rules, not on the carrier alone. Contact your airline directly to confirm eligibility, ideally as early as possible.

faqs.answer: Beyond the airline's carrier requirements, check the destination country's current entry requirements for pets, such as microchipping or vaccination documentation, well ahead of travel.

title: Settling a Rabbit or Guinea Pig for a Short Trip
excerpt: Practical preparation for travelling with a rabbit or guinea pig, from choosing the right carrier to keeping a short trip as calm as possible.
content:
Rabbits and guinea pigs are creatures of routine, so any change, including travel, can be unsettling if you don't prepare a little in advance. Unlike dogs and cats, they rarely leave home at all, which means a carrier journey is often a genuinely new experience each time rather than something they've built up any tolerance for.

## Why Small Pets Find Travel Harder

A rabbit or guinea pig's instinct when unsettled is usually to freeze or brace against the ground, which is part of why the carrier itself matters so much here, more than it might for a pet who's used to being handled and moved around regularly.

## When You'll Typically Need to Travel

For most rabbits and guinea pigs, travel is occasional rather than routine: a vet check-up, a house move, or a trip to a boarding service while you're away. Because it happens so rarely, each trip is more likely to feel unfamiliar to your pet than it would for an animal who travels more often, which is exactly why the preparation below matters more here than it might for a dog or cat.

## Preparing the Carrier Before You Leave

### Familiar Bedding Matters

Line the base of the carrier with familiar bedding from their usual home, along with a small handful of hay, so the space smells reassuringly like home rather than new and unfamiliar. Avoid cleaning the carrier too thoroughly right before travel for the same reason, since a strong disinfectant smell can undo some of that familiarity.

### Choosing a Carrier Built for the Right Pet

A solid, non-slip base matters more here than for almost any other pet, since rabbits and guinea pigs need something to grip rather than a mesh floor to sit on. Our [small animal carriers](/carriers/small-animal-carriers) range covers this properly, and our [rabbit carriers](/carriers/small-animal-carriers/rabbit-carriers) and [guinea pig carriers](/carriers/small-animal-carriers/guinea-pig-carriers) ranges are each sized and shaped around their different builds.

## Rabbits and Guinea Pigs Aren't the Same

Although they're often grouped together, rabbits and guinea pigs have different needs in a carrier. Rabbits are generally longer-bodied and benefit from more length to stretch out, while guinea pigs are shorter and wider and tend to settle better in a more enclosed, snugger space. Checking a carrier's specific dimensions against your particular pet, rather than assuming one small animal carrier suits both equally, is worth doing before you buy.

## Keeping the Journey Calm

Keep the journey as smooth and quiet as you reasonably can. Sudden stops, loud music or a lot of handling along the way tend to raise stress levels more than the travel itself. For longer trips, check whether your pet may need access to water or extra ventilation, and always keep the carrier out of direct sunlight in a warm car.

## After You Arrive

Give your rabbit or guinea pig a little time to settle back into familiar surroundings once you're home or at your destination, rather than immediately handling them again. A quiet period with access to their usual food and bedding helps them recover from the journey faster.

## Final Thoughts

A calmer trip for a rabbit or guinea pig comes down mostly to preparation done in advance: familiar bedding, a carrier with a solid base suited to your specific pet, and a smooth, quiet journey rather than anything done on the day itself to compensate. Small pets notice more than owners often expect, so the groundwork genuinely pays off.

faqs.answer: Give them a quiet period with access to their usual food and bedding rather than handling them again straight away, which helps them recover from the journey faster.

title: Soft-Sided vs Hard-Shell Carriers: Which Is Right for You?
excerpt: A practical, side-by-side comparison of soft-sided and hard-shell pet carriers, covering weight, protection, cleaning and which style suits which kind of journey.
content:
Soft-sided and hard-shell carriers each suit different situations, and there's rarely a single right answer, only a better fit for how you actually travel. This guide compares both constructions directly so you can match the choice to your pet and your typical journey, rather than picking whichever looks nicer in photos.

## The Core Trade-Off

Soft-sided carriers are lighter, fold flat for storage and tend to feel less clinical to a nervous pet, since the fabric gives slightly and the shape is less rigid. Hard-shell carriers offer more protection on longer car journeys or when checked as hold luggage, since the rigid shell resists knocks that a soft carrier simply couldn't. Neither is objectively better, it depends on how often you'll use it, how you'll be carrying it, and what kind of journey you're actually planning.

## When Soft-Sided Makes Sense

Soft-sided carriers are usually the better choice for short, everyday trips such as the vet or a quick visit to family, where light weight and easy storage matter more than maximum rigidity. They also tend to suit pets who are already comfortable with handling and don't need the extra structure of a hard shell. Our [soft-sided pet carriers](/carriers/pet-soft-sided-carriers) range covers this construction across every pet we sell.

## When Hard-Shell Makes Sense

Hard-shell carriers hold their shape better when stacked with other luggage or handled by a pet prone to pawing at the sides, and they're also easier to disinfect thoroughly, which matters if you're bringing a new pet home or dealing with an unwell one. Our [hard-sided pet carriers](/carriers/pet-hard-sided-carriers) range covers that sturdier construction instead.

## What About Specific Pets?

If you're shopping specifically for a cat, our [soft-sided cat carriers](/carriers/cat-carriers/soft-sided-cat-carriers) and [hard-sided cat carriers](/carriers/cat-carriers/hard-sided-cat-carriers) ranges cover the same trade-off sized around a cat's typical proportions rather than a general-purpose design.

## A Quick Way to Decide

Ask yourself three questions: how often will you use it, will it mostly travel by hand or by car, and does your pet tend to lean or paw at the sides. Frequent, everyday use with a pet who's already settled in a carrier generally points towards soft-sided. Less frequent but more demanding trips, particularly by car, or a pet who tests the carrier's structure, generally points towards hard-shell.

## Making the Decision

If you're only ever making short trips nearby, a soft carrier will usually serve you well, and it's the easier option to store when it's not in use. If you travel further afield more often, or your pet needs a bit more structure and protection, particularly for car travel or occasions where the carrier might get knocked about, it may be worth having a hard-shell option too. Some owners end up with one of each, using a soft carrier for routine trips and a hard shell for anything more demanding.

## Final Thoughts

The right choice comes down to how often you'll use the carrier and what kind of journey you're actually planning, not which construction sounds sturdier on paper. A soft-sided carrier suits regular, everyday use well, while a hard shell earns its place when protection and structure matter more than convenience.

faqs.question: Which is safer, soft-sided or hard-shell?
faqs.answer: Both are safe for everyday use when properly secured. Hard-shell offers more physical protection against knocks, which matters more for car travel or busy handling, while soft-sided is perfectly adequate for calmer, shorter trips.

faqs.question: Can I use a soft-sided carrier for car journeys?
faqs.answer: Yes, many owners do, though a hard-shell carrier generally offers more structure if your journeys are frequent or your pet is boisterous. Check our pet carriers for car travel range for options built specifically for stability in a vehicle.

faqs.question: Are hard-shell carriers harder to store?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, since most don't fold flat the way soft-sided carriers do. Some split into two halves for slightly flatter storage, worth checking on the specific product.

faqs.question: Is one style better for a nervous pet?
faqs.answer: This varies by individual pet. Some feel more settled in a solid, enclosed shell, while others prefer the slight give of soft-sided fabric. There's no universal answer, it depends on your pet's own preference.

faqs.question: Do I need both types?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, but some owners keep a soft-sided carrier for routine trips and a hard-shell for less frequent, more demanding journeys such as longer car trips.
